JSON: Name: dasp_night_depth Title: Adversarial transfer of spatiotemporal priors for self-supervised nighttime monocular depth estimation Short Hypothesis: Transferring daytime-derived spatiotemporal priors into nighttime self-supervised training via an adversarial discriminator that learns temporal and axial spatial patterns, combined with a 3D projection consistency loss, reduces per-pixel depth estimation error on nighttime monocular sequences relative to an otherwise-identical self-supervised baseline without such priors. Related Work: Existing work on monocular depth estimation follows three relevant threads. First, self-supervised multi-frame methods recover depth and pose from monocular video using photometric and geometric consistency; they handle static scenes well but degrade on dynamic regions and low-visibility frames. Second, approaches addressing nighttime or adverse illumination use domain adaptation, image enhancement, or daytime-derived priors to bridge day-night appearance gaps; these improve daytime-to-night transfer but often treat frames independently and do not exploit temporal consistency across sequences. Third, methods for dynamics handle moving objects using optical flow, masks, or object-motion modeling, but they either add supervision complexity or rely on unstable heuristics in low-light. GAN-based and self-distillation techniques have been used to generate or regularize hard nighttime samples, yet they tend to focus on local appearance translation instead of explicit spatiotemporal structural priors. Overall limitations: lack of explicit, learned spatiotemporal priors from daytime, weak enforcement of 3D geometric consistency across frames, instability in dynamic/blurred regions, and limited evaluations on multiple nighttime driving datasets. Abstract: Nighttime monocular depth estimation suffers from low visibility, illumination variance and dynamic scene blur. We propose a self-supervised framework that transfers spatiotemporal priors learned from daytime data into nighttime depth estimation via adversarial adaptation and enforces cross-view 3D consistency during training. The discriminator is built from repeated Spatiotemporal Priors Learning Blocks (SPLB) that contain a Spatial-based Temporal Learning Module (STLM) to capture motion-related temporal differences and an Axial Spatial Learning Module (ASLM) to capture multiscale axial spatial structure; a pre-trained daytime depth model provides depth sequences as priors. A self-supervised branch predicts nighttime depth and pose and is optimized using photometric, smoothness, geometric consistency and a novel 3D projection consistency loss that projects source and target pixels into a shared 3D coordinate space for direct depth discrepancy minimization. The main contribution is combining adversarial transfer of explicit spatiotemporal priors with a 3D projection consistency objective to improve robustness in textureless, low-light, and blurry dynamic regions. The expected outcome is systematically lower depth error and improved structural coherence on nighttime driving datasets. Experiments: Datasets: Oxford RobotCar (use sequence 2014-12-16-18-44-24, left front stereo images cropped to 1152x672; training: first five splits excluding stationary frames ~19k frames, test: 411 frames from splits 5-6 with LiDAR-derived dense test depth) and nuScenes (select 60 nighttime scenes, crop to 1536x768; training: >10k nighttime frames, test: 500 frames with top-LiDAR-derived test depth). Baselines: Monodepth2 trained on nighttime data, ADDS, RNW, STEPS, SRNSD, PromptMono, ACDepth, and an ablated Monodepth2 with pretrained daytime model but no SPLB or 3D loss. Metrics: AbsRel, SqRel, RMSE, RMSElog, and δ thresholds (δ<1.25, δ<1.252, δ<1.253). Training setup: pretrain daytime generator (Monodepth2) on daytime splits; nighttime generator initialized and trained with self-supervised losses and adversarial adaptation for 50 epochs; optimizer Adam, batch size 8, initial lr 3e-5 warmed to 1e-4 after 500 iterations then halved at epoch 15; run each experiment with 3 random seeds and report mean±std. Core comparisons and ablations: (A) Full method vs. baselines on both datasets and both depth ranges (40m, 60m). (B) Ablation 1: remove adversarial discriminator (no daytime priors). (C) Ablation 2: remove 3D projection consistency loss. (D) Ablation 3: use STLM only. (E) Ablation 4: use ASLM only. (F) Ablation 5: remove both STLM and ASLM (standard discriminator). (G) Ablation 6: vary number of daytime prior frames fed to discriminator {1,2,3,5}. (H) Ablation 7: vary SPLB depth (number of stacked blocks) {1,2,4}. (I) Measure inference throughput on RTX 3090 and NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and memory usage. Analysis: per-class error on dynamic vs static regions, qualitative visualizations, and paired statistical significance tests (paired t-test, p<0.05) comparing full method vs strongest baseline. Risk Factors and Limitations: Adversarial training instability leading to mode collapse or failure to transfer useful priors; sensitivity to the quality of the pretrained daytime depth model (errors in daytime priors will bias nighttime predictions); increased computational and memory cost from SPLB modules and multi-frame inputs, limiting real-time deployment on resource-constrained hardware; 3D projection consistency requires accurate relative poses—pose estimation errors or large occlusions will corrupt the 3D loss; LiDAR-derived test depth is sparse or noisy causing biased evaluation and limited ground-truth coverage in textureless regions; method may not generalize to sensors with different intrinsics or camera rigs without retuning; degraded performance under extreme low-light, severe motion blur, or dense fog/rain where photometric cues and temporal continuity are weak; dependence on matching day/night scene content distribution—geographic or seasonal domain shifts may reduce effectiveness.
